mainEntity.name: What is an interface in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An interface in Java is a completely abstract type that defines a CONTRACT — a set of method signatures that implementing classes must provide. Declared with the 'interface' keyword, it specifies WHAT a class must do, without dictating HOW. Since Java 8, interfaces can also contain default methods (concrete implementations) and static methods. Since Java 9, private methods are allowed as internal helpers. Interfaces are the primary mechanism for achieving multiple type implementation in Java.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Interface: defines a pure contract; all fields are implicitly public static final (constants); abstract methods are implicitly public; supports multiple implementation (a class can implement many interfaces); no constructor; default/static/private methods allowed since Java 8/9. Abstract class: can have both abstract and concrete methods; can have instance fields with any modifier; supports only single inheritance; has constructors; better for sharing common implementation across related classes. Rule: use interface for defining a capability/contract (Serializable, Comparable). Use abstract class for a common base with shared state/behaviour among closely related types.

mainEntity.name: What is a functional interface in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A functional interface is an interface with exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It may have any number of default or static methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation enforces this at compile time. Functional interfaces are the foundation of Java 8 lambda expressions and method references — a lambda is essentially an anonymous implementation of the single abstract method. Built-in examples: Runnable (run()), Callable (call()), Comparator (compare()), Predicate (test()), Function (apply()), Consumer (accept()), Supplier (get()).

mainEntity.name: What are default methods in Java interfaces?

acceptedAnswer.text: Default methods (Java 8+) are concrete method implementations inside an interface, declared with the 'default' keyword. They solve the API evolution problem: adding a new method to an existing interface would break all implementing classes. With default methods, a new method can be added with a default implementation — existing implementors work unchanged and can override the default if needed. They also enable interface composition patterns. Conflict: if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method, the class MUST explicitly override to resolve the ambiguity.

mainEntity.name: Can an interface extend another interface in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — an interface CAN extend one or MORE other interfaces using the 'extends' keyword (not 'implements'). This is interface inheritance and it allows building rich interface hierarchies. Example: 'public interface ReadWriteRepository extends ReadRepository, WriteRepository'. An interface that extends multiple interfaces inherits all their abstract methods and default methods. A class implementing the derived interface must implement ALL inherited abstract methods from the entire hierarchy.

sections.title: What is an Interface in Java?

blocks.text: An interface in Java is a reference type — similar to a class — that defines a contract: a set of method signatures that any implementing class must honour. An interface specifies WHAT must be done, without prescribing HOW. It is the purest expression of abstraction in Java — separating the definition of a capability from any specific implementation of that capability.

Think of an interface as a legal contract. The interface says: 'Any class that signs this contract agrees to provide these methods.' A Printable interface contract says every implementing class will provide a print() method. A Comparable contract says every implementing class will provide a compareTo() method. The interface does not care how — only that the method exists and is callable.

Interfaces have evolved significantly across Java versions. In Java 7 and earlier, interfaces could only contain abstract methods and constants. Java 8 added default methods (concrete implementations) and static methods — solving the API evolution problem. Java 9 added private methods for internal interface helper logic. Java 17 introduced sealed interfaces — restricting which classes can implement them. Modern Java interfaces are rich, powerful constructs.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Interface at a Glance
blocks.text: An interface in Java can contain: (1) Abstract methods — implicitly public abstract; implementing classes MUST provide the body. (2) Constants — implicitly public static final; shared by all implementors. (3) Default methods (Java 8+) — concrete implementations with the 'default' keyword; can be overridden. (4) Static methods (Java 8+) — belong to the interface itself; called via InterfaceName.method(). (5) Private methods (Java 9+) — internal helpers for default/static methods; NOT inherited. A class uses 'implements' to adopt an interface's contract. An interface uses 'extends' to inherit from other interfaces. A class can implement multiple interfaces simultaneously.

sections.title: Interface Declaration & Syntax — Anatomy of a Java Interface

blocks.text: Declaring a Java interface follows a specific structure. Understanding the syntax and implicit rules for each element prevents the most common interface-related compile errors.

items.title: Full Syntax
Interface Naming Conventions
items.text:
• PascalCase — same as classes
• Name as a capability/adjective: Runnable, Serializable, Closeable, Comparable, Iterable
• Or as a noun representing a role: Repository, Service, Handler, Processor
• Avoid 'IInterface' prefix (Hungarian notation) — not idiomatic Java
• Good: Payable, Sortable, EventListener, NotificationSender
• Avoid vague names: Manager, Helper, Util as interface names

items.title: Interface Modifiers
items.text:
Access: public (visible everywhere) or default/package-private (same package only). Top-level interfaces CANNOT be private or protected.
Non-access:
• abstract — implicit; every interface is abstract (no need to write)
• sealed (Java 17+) — restricts permitted implementors
• @FunctionalInterface — annotation validating exactly one abstract method
Note: 'abstract interface' is redundant — omit 'abstract'; the compiler adds it.

sections.title: Implementing an Interface — The implements Keyword

blocks.text: A class adopts an interface's contract using the implements keyword. Once a class declares it implements an interface, it must provide a concrete body for every abstract method in that interface — or declare itself abstract to defer the obligation to its subclasses. Failing to implement all abstract methods is a compile-time error.

items.title: implements Syntax
Implementation Rules
items.text:
1. MUST implement ALL abstract methods — or declare the class abstract.
2. Implemented methods MUST be public — interface methods are implicitly public; narrowing is a compile error.
3. @Override is recommended — catches method signature typos.
4. Can inherit default methods without overriding — but MUST override if two interfaces provide the same default method.
5. Can use super to call a specific interface's default: InterfaceName.super.method().

items.title: IS-A Contract
items.text: When a class implements an interface, 'instanceof' returns true for that interface type. A UPIGateway that implements PaymentGateway IS-A PaymentGateway. This enables polymorphism through interfaces — code written against the interface type works with ANY implementing class, decoupling callers from implementations.

sections.title: Default Methods (Java 8+) — Evolving APIs Without Breaking Changes

blocks.text: Default methods are concrete method implementations inside an interface, declared with the default keyword. Introduced in Java 8, they solved a critical API design challenge: before Java 8, adding a new method to a published interface immediately broke every existing implementation. With default methods, a new method can carry a sensible default implementation — existing implementations continue working unchanged.

items.title: Why Default Methods Exist — API Evolution
items.text: Before Java 8: adding forEach() to java.util.Collection would require updating every custom Collection implementation in the world. After Java 8: forEach() was added as a default method — existing implementations inherited a working forEach() using Iterator internally. No existing code broke. This is why the Java 8 Stream API integration was possible without breaking decades of existing Collection code.

items.title: Default Method Resolution Rules
items.text:
When multiple sources provide a method with the same signature, Java resolves in this priority order:
1. Class or superclass method WINS over any interface default.
2. More specific interface wins over less specific (derived interface over base).
3. If two unrelated interfaces have the same default — the implementing class MUST explicitly override to resolve the conflict (compile error otherwise).
4. Call a specific interface's default: InterfaceName.super.methodName().

items.title: Default Methods for Interface Composition
items.text: Default methods enable a form of 'mixin' — small, reusable behaviour that can be mixed into any class implementing the interface. Example: a 'Loggable' interface with a default log() method can be implemented by any class to gain logging capability. A 'Retryable' interface can provide a default executeWithRetry() used by any service. This is the foundation of modern Java's composable design.

blocks.title: 💡 Class Always Wins Over Interface Default
blocks.text: If a class (or its superclass) defines a method with the same signature as an interface's default method, the class's version ALWAYS takes priority — even if the class doesn't explicitly override the interface method. Example: if class Animal defines 'void describe()' and a class Dog extends Animal and implements Describable (which has 'default void describe()'), Dog inherits Animal.describe(), not Describable.describe(). The class hierarchy always beats the interface default.

sections.title: Static Methods in Interfaces (Java 8+)

blocks.text: Static methods in interfaces (Java 8+) belong to the interface itself — not to implementing classes or objects. They are called directly on the interface: InterfaceName.methodName(). They are NOT inherited by implementing classes and cannot be overridden. They serve as namespace-organised utility methods tightly associated with the interface's purpose.

items.title: Purpose of Static Interface Methods
items.text: Factory methods: 'Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)' — creates a Comparator without needing a separate utility class. Validation utilities: 'PaymentGateway.validateRequest(req)'. Default instance creation: 'Executor.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()'. Before Java 8, these would live in separate utility classes (Collections, Arrays). Static interface methods place utilities where they logically belong — on the interface itself.

items.title: Static Methods Are NOT Inherited
items.text: Unlike default methods, static interface methods are NOT inherited by implementing classes. If UPIGateway implements PaymentGateway, calling 'UPIGateway.validateRequest(req)' is a compile error — it must be 'PaymentGateway.validateRequest(req)'. This is by design — static methods are tied to the interface namespace, not to instances. This avoids confusion with method hiding.

sections.title: Private Methods in Interfaces (Java 9+)

blocks.text: Private methods in interfaces (Java 9+) are concrete methods inside an interface that are only accessible within the interface itself. They are NOT inherited by implementing classes and NOT accessible from outside the interface. Their sole purpose is to eliminate code duplication among default and static methods within the same interface.

items.title: Two Types of Private Interface Methods
items.text:
private instance methods: can be called by default methods in the same interface. They have access to 'this' (the implementing object) via the default method context.
private static methods: can be called by static methods AND default methods in the same interface. They cannot access 'this'. Use private static when the helper doesn't need the implementing object's state.

items.title: Why Private Methods Matter
items.text: Before Java 9: if two default methods shared common logic, you had to either duplicate the code or expose a helper as another default method (polluting the interface's public API with implementation details). Java 9 private methods solve this cleanly — the shared logic is extracted to a private helper that is invisible to implementing classes and external callers.

items.title: Private Method Rules
items.text:
1. Must have a body — cannot be abstract.
2. Cannot be default (the keywords cannot be combined).
3. private instance methods: callable by default methods.
4. private static methods: callable by both default and static methods.
5. NOT inherited — not visible outside the interface.
6. Cannot be accessed via InterfaceName.super — they are implementation details, not contract.

sections.title: Implementing Multiple Interfaces — Java's Answer to Multiple Inheritance

blocks.text: A Java class can implement multiple interfaces simultaneously — this is how Java achieves the benefits of multiple inheritance without the Diamond Problem. Each interface the class implements adds a new type to the class, enabling extremely flexible polymorphic code. A class can declare its capabilities through multiple interface implementations, and callers can use whichever type fits their need.

items.title: Multiple IS-A Relationships
items.text: When a class implements multiple interfaces, it satisfies multiple IS-A relationships simultaneously. A Duck class that implements Flyable, Swimmable, and Quackable IS-A Flyable, IS-A Swimmable, and IS-A Quackable. Each interface type can be used as the reference type for a Duck variable. This lets different parts of the codebase interact with a Duck only through the capability they care about.

items.title: Diamond Problem — How Java Resolves It
items.text: When two interfaces provide the same default method and a class implements both, Java forces the implementor to resolve the conflict explicitly by overriding the method. Inside the override, the class can call a specific interface's default using 'InterfaceName.super.methodName()'. This explicit resolution makes the intent clear and avoids hidden ambiguity — unlike C++ multiple inheritance where the conflict resolution can be subtle.

items.title: Interface Segregation Principle
items.text: Don't force clients to depend on methods they don't use. Instead of one fat interface, create multiple focused ones. A Printer that prints documents should implement Printable. A Scanner that scans should implement Scannable. An all-in-one device implements both. Clients that only print use Printable — they're unaffected if Scannable changes. This is the 'I' in SOLID.

sections.title: Interface Extending Interface — Building Rich Type Hierarchies

blocks.text: An interface can extend one or more other interfaces using the extends keyword (NOT implements). This creates an interface hierarchy where the derived interface inherits all abstract and default methods from its parent interfaces and can add new methods. A class implementing the derived interface must satisfy the contracts of the entire hierarchy.

sections.title: Functional Interfaces & Lambdas — The Heart of Modern Java

blocks.text: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It may have any number of default, static, or private methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation signals intent and enforces the single-abstract-method constraint at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target types for lambda expressions and method references — Java's most significant feature addition since generics.

items.title: Built-in Functional Interfaces (java.util.function)
items.text:
Java 8 ships with 43 functional interfaces in java.util.function. The 4 core categories:
• Predicate<T>: T → boolean — test(T t)
• Function<T,R>: T → R — apply(T t)
• Consumer<T>: T → void — accept(T t)
• Supplier<T>: () → T — get()
Specialised variants: BiFunction<T,U,R>, UnaryOperator<T>, BinaryOperator<T>, IntPredicate, LongFunction, etc.

sections.title: Marker Interfaces — Tagging Without Methods

blocks.text: A marker interface (also called a tag interface) is an interface with no methods and no fields. Its only purpose is to mark or tag a class as having a certain property — to communicate metadata about the class to the JVM, frameworks, or other code. The tag is detectable via instanceof or reflection.

items.title: Built-in Marker Interfaces
items.text:
java.io.Serializable: marks a class whose objects can be converted to a byte stream. JVM's ObjectOutputStream checks instanceof Serializable before serialising.
java.lang.Cloneable: marks a class whose objects can be cloned via Object.clone(). Without this, clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException.
java.util.RandomAccess: marks List implementations supporting constant-time positional access — Collections.binarySearch() uses instanceof RandomAccess to choose the optimal algorithm.

items.title: Modern Alternative — Annotations
items.text: Since Java 5, annotations are the preferred way to tag classes with metadata. '@Override', '@Deprecated', '@Entity', '@Service' all serve as modern 'markers'. Annotations are more powerful: they can carry data, be targeted at specific element types, and be processed at compile time, runtime, or both. Marker interfaces are still used in legacy code and for IS-A checks via instanceof.

items.title: Custom Marker Interface Use Cases
items.text: In domain-driven design: 'interface DomainEvent {}' — marks all events. Frameworks check 'if (obj instanceof DomainEvent)' to route appropriately. Security: 'interface Sensitive {}' — marks DTOs containing sensitive data; a serialisation filter checks for this marker. Audit: 'interface Auditable {}' — an AOP aspect intercepts calls on Auditable classes. Each is simple and effective for type-based dispatch.

blocks.text: Choosing between an interface and an abstract class is one of the most common design decisions in Java OOP. Both provide abstraction, but they serve fundamentally different purposes. sections.title: Sealed Interfaces (Java 17+) — Controlled Extensibility

blocks.text: Sealed interfaces (Java 17, JEP 409) restrict which classes or interfaces can implement them. Declared with the sealed keyword and a permits clause, they give API designers controlled extensibility — the interface is open for use but closed for implementation to an explicit, known set of types. This enables exhaustive pattern matching in switch expressions.

items.title: Sealed Interface Rules
items.text:
1. Declared with 'sealed' + 'permits ClassName, ...' listing every permitted implementor.
2. Permitted classes MUST directly implement or extend the sealed interface.
3. Permitted classes MUST be in the same package (or module) as the sealed interface.
4. Each permitted class must be one of: 'final' (no further subclassing), 'sealed' (further restricts), or 'non-sealed' (opens back up for extension).

items.title: Why Sealed Interfaces Matter
items.text: Enables exhaustive switch pattern matching — if all permitted types are known, the compiler can verify that a switch covers all cases without a default. This is how Java models algebraic data types (sum types). Example: a Shape sealed interface with Circle, Rectangle, Triangle as permitted types — a switch on Shape must handle all three, and the compiler enforces this. This is safer than open hierarchies where new subclasses can appear unexpectedly.

items.title: Sealed Interfaces + Records
items.text: Java records (Java 16+) pair beautifully with sealed interfaces. Records are implicitly final, making them perfect permitted types — they carry data without mutable state. Pattern: 'sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle' where each is a record: 'record Circle(double radius) implements Shape'. This is modern Java's concise, type-safe algebraic data type pattern used in compilers, parsers, and domain event hierarchies.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Trip Everyone Up

blocks.text: These interface-related mistakes appear consistently in Java beginner and intermediate code. Each one either causes a compile-time error or a subtle design problem that surfaces later during maintenance.

blocks.label: InterfaceMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Making interface method non-public in implementing class
interface Printable { void print(); } // implicitly public
// void print() { } // ❌ Compile error — reduces public to default
public void print() { System.out.println("Printing"); } // ✅ Must be public
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Treating interface constants as instance variables
int MAX_RETRY = 3; // implicitly public static final
// int MAX_RETRY = 5; // ❌ Cannot reassign — it's final
// Worse: accessing it via 'this.MAX_RETRY' is misleading
System.out.println(MAX_RETRY); // ✅ Direct access — but use Config.MAX_RETRY
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Writing 'abstract' explicitly on interface methods
public abstract void start(); // 'public abstract' is redundant — already implicit
// interface B implements A { } // ❌ Compile error — interfaces use 'extends'
interface B extends A { void methodB(); } // ✅ Correct
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Forgetting to implement all abstract methods
interface Flyable { void fly(); void land(); }
//     // ❌ Compile error: Eagle is not abstract and does not override land()
// ✅ Fix: implement both, or declare class abstract
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Two interfaces with conflicting defaults — not resolving
interface Logger   { default void log() { System.out.println("Logger"); } }
interface Auditor  { default void log() { System.out.println("Auditor"); } }
// class Service implements Logger, Auditor { } // ❌ Compile error — ambiguous default
Logger.super.log();  // Pick one, or write your own
// ❌ MISTAKE 7: Calling interface static method via implementing class
interface MathOps { static int square(int n) { return n * n; } }
// Calculator.square(5); // ❌ Compile error — static interface methods not inherited
MathOps.square(5); // ✅ Called on the interface itself

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These interface anti-patterns are consistently rejected in professional code reviews. Each violates design principles and makes codebases harder to maintain, test, and evolve.

items.title: Constant Interface Anti-Pattern
items.text: Using an interface purely to hold constants that classes implement to 'inherit' them. Example: 'interface Constants { int MAX=100; String BASE_URL="..."; }'. Implementing classes inherit these constants but now have 'Constants' as a public IS-A type — a meaningless API commitment. Classes should not implement interfaces just for constant access. Fix: use a final utility class with private constructor: 'public final class AppConstants { private AppConstants(){} public static final int MAX = 100; }'

items.title: Fat Interface — Violating ISP
items.text: An interface with 20+ methods that no single class realistically needs all of. Implementing classes must provide empty/stub implementations for irrelevant methods. Any change to the interface forces updates across all implementors. Fix: apply Interface Segregation Principle — split into focused, cohesive interfaces. A UserService doesn't need to implement UserRepository, UserNotificationService, and UserAuditService all in one contract.

items.title: Overusing Default Methods as Implementation
items.text: Adding substantial business logic as default methods, effectively turning the interface into a partial abstract class. Interfaces should define contracts and optionally provide thin convenience defaults. When a default method is long, complex, or depends on many other methods — it signals the logic belongs in an abstract class or a shared utility. The interface is becoming a tangled mix of contract and implementation.

items.title: Missing @FunctionalInterface Annotation
items.text: Defining an interface intended as a lambda target without @FunctionalInterface. Without the annotation, accidentally adding a second abstract method is a compile-but-silently-breaks situation — all lambdas targeting that interface now fail. @FunctionalInterface is a defensive annotation: if someone adds a second abstract method, it immediately fails to compile. Always annotate intentional functional interfaces.

items.title: Interface for Everything — Even Non-Contractual Types
items.text: Some developers create an interface for every class 'just in case'. 'UserService' interface with 'UserServiceImpl' as the only implementation forever. This adds a layer of abstraction with no value — every change requires updating both the interface and the class. Create interfaces when: multiple implementations exist or are expected, you want to decouple callers from implementations, or you're designing a library API. Don't create 1:1 interface-class pairs reflexively.

items.title: Exposing Implementation Detail Through Interface
items.text: Adding framework-specific or technology-specific methods to a domain interface. Example: 'interface UserRepository { ... ; EntityManager getEntityManager(); }'. Now every caller of UserRepository is coupled to JPA/Hibernate. The interface should model the domain contract only. Technology details belong in the implementing class. Keep interfaces pure — they represent what the caller needs, not what the implementation uses.

sections.title: Java Interface Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, campus placements, and OCPJP certification exams.

items.q: Q1. What is an interface in Java? How is it different from a class?
items.a: An interface is a reference type that defines a contract — a set of method signatures that implementing classes must provide. Unlike a class, an interface: (1) Cannot be instantiated directly. (2) Has no constructors. (3) All fields are implicitly public static final (constants). (4) Traditional abstract methods are implicitly public abstract. (5) A class can implement multiple interfaces simultaneously (vs single class inheritance). (6) Since Java 8+: can have default, static methods. Since Java 9+: can have private methods. Interface represents CAPABILITY/BEHAVIOUR contract. Class represents a TYPE with state and behaviour.

items.q: Q2. What are default methods in interfaces? Why were they introduced?
items.a: Default methods (Java 8+) are concrete method implementations inside an interface, declared with the 'default' keyword. They were introduced to solve the API evolution problem: before Java 8, adding a method to a published interface broke all existing implementing classes. With default methods, a new method can carry a default implementation — existing implementors inherit a working default and can override if needed. This enabled Java 8's Stream API to be added to the existing Collection interface (forEach(), spliterator(), stream()) without breaking all existing Collection implementations. Conflict resolution: if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method, it MUST explicitly override to resolve the ambiguity.

items.q: Q3. Can an interface extend another interface? Can it extend a class?
items.a: An interface CAN extend one or MORE other interfaces using 'extends' (NOT 'implements'). Interface inheritance allows building rich type hierarchies — 'interface ReadWriteRepository extends ReadRepository, WriteRepository'. An interface inherits all abstract methods and default methods from parent interfaces. A class implementing the derived interface must implement ALL inherited abstract methods from the entire hierarchy. An interface CANNOT extend a class — only interfaces can be extended by interfaces. Extends is for class-to-class and interface-to-interface. Implements is for class-to-interface.

items.q: Q4. What is a functional interface? What is @FunctionalInterface?
items.a: A functional interface has exactly ONE abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have any number of default, static, or private methods. @FunctionalInterface is an annotation that enforces this at compile time — if someone accidentally adds a second abstract method, the compile fails immediately. Functional interfaces are the target types for lambda expressions and method references. Built-in examples: Runnable (run()), Callable (call()), Comparator (compare()), and the entire java.util.function package — Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction, etc. Without @FunctionalInterface, a class can still target an interface with one abstract method as a lambda — the annotation is defensive documentation, not a technical requirement.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?
items.a: Interface: defines a capability/contract; fields are public static final constants only; methods are implicitly public; no constructors; no instance state; a class can implement multiple interfaces; used for cross-cutting capabilities (Serializable, Comparable, Runnable). Abstract class: can have both abstract and concrete methods; can have instance fields with any modifier; has constructors; supports only single inheritance; can have mutable state; used for closely related types sharing common implementation. Rule: use interface for 'can-do' capabilities any unrelated class might need. Use abstract class for 'is-a' base type with shared state and behaviour among closely related classes. Best pattern: interface for the contract, abstract class for partial implementation (e.g., AbstractList implements List).

items.q: Q6. Can interfaces have constructors in Java?
items.a: No — interfaces CANNOT have constructors. Constructors are used to initialise object state (instance fields), but interfaces have no instance state (no instance fields — only public static final constants). Since interfaces cannot be instantiated directly (you cannot write 'new Runnable()'), there is no object to initialise. The 'new InterfaceName()' syntax only works for anonymous class instantiation — not a true interface constructor call. If you need shared initialisation logic for all implementors, put it in an abstract class that implements the interface.

items.q: Q7. What happens when a class implements two interfaces with the same default method?
items.a: It is a compile-time error — Java cannot automatically choose which default to use. The implementing class MUST explicitly override the method to resolve the conflict. Inside the override, the class can: (1) Choose one interface's default: 'A.super.method()' or 'B.super.method()'. (2) Write a completely new implementation. (3) Call both in sequence. This explicit resolution makes intent clear. Contrast: if a class extends a superclass that provides a concrete method AND implements an interface with a default method of the same name — the SUPERCLASS METHOD WINS. Class hierarchy always beats interface defaults.

items.q: Q8. What are marker interfaces? Give examples and their modern alternative.
items.a: A marker interface has no methods and no fields — its sole purpose is to tag a class as having a certain property, detectable via instanceof or reflection. Examples: java.io.Serializable (enables serialisation), java.lang.Cloneable (enables clone()), java.util.RandomAccess (signals O(1) index access for List). Modern alternative: annotations. @Entity, @Service, @Override, @Deprecated all serve as markers with more power — they can carry data, be targeted at specific elements, and be processed by annotation processors at compile time or runtime via reflection. Marker interfaces remain relevant for IS-A type checks (instanceof Serializable) while annotations are preferred for most new metadata needs.

items.q: Q9. What are sealed interfaces (Java 17+)? How do they help?
items.a: Sealed interfaces (Java 17, JEP 409) restrict which classes or interfaces can implement them, declared with 'sealed' and 'permits ClassName, ...'. Benefits: (1) Exhaustive pattern matching — the compiler knows all permitted types and can verify a switch covers all cases without a default clause. (2) Controlled extensibility — the interface is available for use everywhere but only specific types can implement it. (3) Domain modelling — models algebraic data types (sum types). Each permitted type must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. Combined with records, they enable concise, type-safe domain event and result type hierarchies. Switch pattern matching in Java 21 fully leverages sealed interfaces for exhaustive, compiler-verified dispatch.

items.q: Q10. Can we declare variables inside an interface? What are their implicit modifiers?
items.a: Yes — variables declared inside an interface are implicitly 'public static final' — i.e., they are constants. This happens regardless of what modifiers you write. 'int MAX = 100;' in an interface is automatically 'public static final int MAX = 100;'. Consequences: (1) They must be initialised at the point of declaration — no lazy initialisation. (2) They cannot be reassigned — final. (3) They are accessed via the interface name: InterfaceName.CONSTANT. (4) They are inherited by implementing classes, but accessing via the class name is misleading. Anti-pattern: creating an interface purely to hold constants (Constant Interface Anti-Pattern) — use a final utility class instead.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Interface Knowledge

blocks.text: Attempt each question independently before reading the answer — active recall significantly improves retention and understanding.

items.a: Output: 'Base hello'. This demonstrates the default method resolution rule: a class's (or superclass's) concrete method ALWAYS wins over an interface's default method. Child extends Base (which has a concrete hello()) and implements Greet (which has a default hello()). Java resolves to Base.hello() — the class hierarchy beats the interface default. No compile error — no ambiguity because the rule is unambiguous. If Base did NOT have hello(), then Greet's default would be inherited and 'Interface hello' would print.

Two issues: (1) 'protected void draw()' — COMPILE ERROR. Interface abstract methods are implicitly public. Implementing them with 'protected' narrows the access modifier — illegal. Fix: 'public void draw()'. (2) 'Canvas.staticHelper()' — COMPILE ERROR. Static interface methods are NOT inherited by implementing classes. They can only be called on the interface itself. Fix: 'Drawable.staticHelper()'. Corrected class: 'public class Canvas implements Drawable { public void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing"); } public void render() { Drawable.staticHelper(); } }'

items.q: 3. Design a functional interface 'StringTransformer' that takes a String and returns a String. Use it with lambdas to: (a) uppercase, (b) reverse, (c) trim+lowercase. Then compose them.
items.a: @FunctionalInterface interface StringTransformer { String transform(String input); default StringTransformer andThen(StringTransformer next) { return input -> next.transform(this.transform(input)); } }  Usage: StringTransformer toUpper   = String::toUpperCase; StringTransformer reverse    = s -> new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(); StringTransformer normalise  = s -> s.trim().toLowerCase();  StringTransformer pipeline = normalise.andThen(toUpper).andThen(reverse);  System.out.println(toUpper.transform("hello"));     // HELLO System.out.println(reverse.transform("Java"));       // avaJ System.out.println(normalise.transform("  HELLO  ")); // hello System.out.println(pipeline.transform("  Java  "));   // avaj  Note: andThen() as a default method enables composition just like Function.andThen() in java.util.function.

items.q: 4. Two interfaces A and B both have 'default void log()'. Class C implements both. Show how to resolve the conflict — (a) using A's version, (b) using B's version, (c) writing a completely new version.
items.a: interface A { default void log() { System.out.println("A log"); } } interface B { default void log() { System.out.println("B log"); } }  class C implements A, B { @Override public void log() { // Option a: use A's version A.super.log(); // Option b: use B's version // B.super.log(); // Option c: completely new // System.out.println("C custom log"); } }  If C does NOT override log(), it is a COMPILE ERROR — Java cannot choose between A's and B's defaults. The @Override and explicit resolution is mandatory. You can also call both: A.super.log(); B.super.log(); System.out.println("C own message"); — all three in sequence.

This is the Constant Interface Anti-Pattern — an interface used purely for constants. Problems: (1) DatabaseService now has 'AppConstants' as a public IS-A type — a meaningless API commitment that leaks implementation detail. (2) Every class needing constants must implement the interface, polluting their type hierarchy. (3) API_KEY as a public interface constant is visible globally — security concern. Fix: use a final utility class with a private constructor. public final class AppConstants { private AppConstants() {} public static final String DB_URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/app"; public static final int MAX_CONNECTIONS = 10; private static final String API_KEY = "secret-key-12345"; // private! } — DatabaseService removes 'implements AppConstants' and uses 'AppConstants.DB_URL' directly.

items.q: 6. Implement a sealed interface 'Result<T>' with two permitted records: 'Success<T>' (holds a value T) and 'Failure<T>' (holds an error message String). Write a method that uses exhaustive switch pattern matching.
items.a: public sealed interface Result<T> permits Result.Success, Result.Failure { record Success<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {} record Failure<T>(String error) implements Result<T> {}  static <T> Result<T> of(java.util.function.Supplier<T> supplier) { try { return new Success<>(supplier.get()); } catch (Exception e) { return new Failure<>(e.getMessage()); } }  default boolean isSuccess() { return this instanceof Success; } default T getOrThrow() { return switch (this) { case Success<T> s -> s.value(); case Failure<T> f -> throw new RuntimeException(f.error()); }; } }  Usage: Result<Integer> r1 = Result.of(() -> Integer.parseInt("42")); Result<Integer> r2 = Result.of(() -> Integer.parseInt("abc")); String msg1 = switch (r1) { case Result.Success<Integer> s -> "Value: " + s.value(); case Result.Failure<Integer> f -> "Error: " + f.error(); }; System.out.println(msg1); // Value: 42

items.q: 7. Explain why 'new Runnable() { ... }' is an anonymous class and how it relates to a lambda. Show both forms.
items.a: Runnable is a functional interface with one abstract method: 'void run()'. Before Java 8, the only way to provide an inline implementation was an anonymous class: Runnable r1 = new Runnable() { @Override public void run() { System.out.println("Running via anonymous class"); } };  With Java 8 lambdas, any functional interface can be implemented with a lambda expression: Runnable r2 = () -> System.out.println("Running via lambda");  Both are semantically equivalent for single-method interfaces. Differences: (1) Lambda is more concise. (2) Lambda captures 'this' from the enclosing class; anonymous class creates its own 'this'. (3) Anonymous class can hold state (fields); lambdas cannot (they capture effectively-final variables). (4) Anonymous classes can extend abstract classes; lambdas target only functional interfaces. (5) Lambdas are implemented via invokedynamic (more efficient); anonymous classes create separate .class files.

items.q: 8. Design an interface hierarchy for a payment system: PaymentGateway (base) → SecurePaymentGateway (adds encryption contract) → InternationalPaymentGateway (adds currency conversion). Show a class implementing the most derived interface.
items.a: interface PaymentGateway { PaymentResult process(double amount, String currency); boolean isAvailable(); default PaymentResult processWithValidation(double amount, String currency) { if (amount <= 0) return PaymentResult.failure("Invalid amount"); if (!isAvailable()) return PaymentResult.failure("Gateway unavailable"); return process(amount, currency); } }  interface SecurePaymentGateway extends PaymentGateway { String encryptPayload(String payload); boolean verifySignature(String payload, String signature); default PaymentResult processSecurely(double amount, String currency, String payload) { String encrypted = encryptPayload(payload); return processWithValidation(amount, currency); } }  interface InternationalPaymentGateway extends SecurePaymentGateway { double convertCurrency(double amount, String from, String to); String[] getSupportedCurrencies(); default PaymentResult processInternational(double amount, String from, String to, String payload) { double converted = convertCurrency(amount, from, to); return processSecurely(converted, to, payload); } }  class StripeGateway implements InternationalPaymentGateway { @Override public PaymentResult process(double a, String c) { return PaymentResult.success("Stripe: " + a + " " + c); } @Override public boolean isAvailable() { return true; } @Override public String encryptPayload(String p) { return "ENC:" + p; } @Override public boolean verifySignature(String p, String s) { return true; } @Override public double convertCurrency(double a, String f, String t) { return a * 0.012; } @Override public String[] getSupportedCurrencies() { return new String[]{"INR","USD","EUR"}; } }

sections.title: Conclusion — Interfaces: The Backbone of Java's Flexibility

blocks.text: Interfaces are the most powerful abstraction mechanism in Java. They enable programming to contracts rather than implementations — the fundamental principle behind testable, extensible, maintainable enterprise software. Every major Java framework — Spring, Hibernate, JUnit, Java EE — is built on carefully designed interface hierarchies that allow any implementation to be swapped without changing the calling code.

Modern Java interfaces are richer than ever: default methods enable API evolution and mixin-style composition; static methods provide namespace-clean factory utilities; private methods enable internal helpers without polluting the public API; functional interfaces power the entire lambda and Stream ecosystem; sealed interfaces bring algebraic data type safety to Java. Mastering interfaces is mastering Java's type system.

items.q: What is an interface in Java?
items.a: An interface in Java is a reference type that defines a contract — a set of method signatures that any implementing class must provide. Declared with the 'interface' keyword, it specifies WHAT must be done without specifying HOW. Since Java 8+, interfaces can also have default methods (concrete implementations), static methods, and since Java 9+, private methods. A class adopts an interface's contract using 'implements'. One class can implement multiple interfaces simultaneously.

items.q: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?
items.a: Interface: defines a capability/contract; fields are public static final constants; no instance state; no constructors; a class can implement multiple interfaces. Abstract class: can have abstract and concrete methods; can have instance fields; has constructors; only single inheritance. Use interface for 'can-do' capabilities any class might need (Serializable, Comparable). Use abstract class for a common base with shared state among closely related types. Best pattern: interface defines the contract, abstract class provides partial implementation.

items.q: What is a functional interface in Java?
items.a: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It may have default, static, or private methods. The @FunctionalInterface annotation enforces the single-abstract-method rule at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target types for lambda expressions and method references. Built-in examples from java.util.function: Predicate<T>, Function<T,R>, Consumer<T>, Supplier<T>, BiFunction<T,U,R>. Any interface with one abstract method can be used as a lambda target, with or without @FunctionalInterface.

items.q: What are default methods in Java interfaces?
items.a: Default methods (Java 8+) are concrete implementations inside an interface, declared with the 'default' keyword. They solve the API evolution problem: adding a new method to a published interface no longer breaks all existing implementations — the default method provides a fallback implementation. Implementing classes can override them. Conflict: if two interfaces provide the same default method, the implementing class MUST explicitly override to resolve the ambiguity, optionally calling a specific interface's default with 'InterfaceName.super.method()'.

items.q: Can an interface extend another interface in Java?
items.a: Yes — an interface can extend one or more other interfaces using 'extends' (not 'implements'). This builds interface hierarchies where the derived interface inherits all abstract and default methods from its parents and can add new ones. A class implementing the derived interface must implement ALL inherited abstract methods from the entire hierarchy. An interface CANNOT extend a class — only interface-to-interface and class-to-class for extends; interface-to-class uses 'implements'.
